tracks.tagline: Build a small layered backend service for tracking books and loans, with real automated tests and applied data-structure work baked into actual features.

1.title: Core Domain Model and In-Memory Service
1.goal: Design the core data model for a library lending service and implement it as clean, layered Python code with an in-memory store, before touching a database or API. Getting the domain logic right first makes everything later easier to test and extend.
learn: Separating domain models from storage and application logic
Designing classes for a small real-world domain (books, copies, loans)
Writing a service layer that enforces business rules
steps: Design `Book` (title, author, isbn) and `Copy` (copy_id, book, is_available) dataclasses, and a `Loan` dataclass (loan_id, copy, borrower_name, due_date, returned).
Set up the project structure with separate modules: `models.py` (dataclasses), `store.py` (in-memory repositories), and `library_service.py` (business logic).
Implement an in-memory `BookRepository` and `LoanRepository` with `add`, `get`, `list` methods backed by plain Python dicts keyed by ID.

Implement `LibraryService.checkout(isbn, borrower_name)` that finds an available copy, marks it unavailable, and creates a `Loan` with a due date 14 days out — raising a clear `NoCopyAvailableError` if none are free.
Implement `LibraryService.return_copy(loan_id)` that marks the loan returned and the copy available again, raising `LoanNotFoundError` for a bad ID.
Install `pytest` and write unit tests covering: successful checkout, checkout with no copies available, successful return, and returning an already-returned loan.
Run `pytest -v` and get all tests passing, then check coverage of your service logic by eye (every method has at least one happy-path and one error-path test).
Commit your code with a README describing the module layout and how to run the tests.
deliverables: A `LibraryService` enforcing checkout/return business rules with custom exceptions
A `pytest` suite covering happy paths and error paths
done_when: `pytest -v` runs and all tests pass with no warnings
Checking out the last available copy of a book then attempting one more raises `NoCopyAvailableError`
Returning a loan twice raises a clear error instead of silently succeeding or crashing
The domain logic in `library_service.py` has no direct dependency on any storage implementation detail beyond calling the repository interface
hints: Keep repositories dumb (just storage and lookups) and business rules (like 'no copies available') entirely in the service layer — this split is what makes layer 3's database swap painless.
Use Python's `dataclasses` module for `Book`, `Copy` and `Loan`; it gives you free `__init__` and `__repr__` with less boilerplate.
The [pytest documentation](https://docs.pytest.org) 'getting started' page has everything needed for this week's tests.
1.stretch: Add a `LibraryService.list_overdue(today)` method that returns all loans past their due date, with a test using a fixed fake 'today' date.
post_highlights: Designed a layered library service with domain models, repositories and business logic cleanly separated
Wrote a pytest suite covering both happy paths and real error conditions
Learned to keep business rules out of the storage layer for easier testing and future changes

2.title: Search, Ranking and a REST API
2.goal: Expose last week's service as a real HTTP API, and add a search feature with relevance ranking — an applied use of sorting and string-matching data structures inside a real feature, not an isolated algorithm exercise.
learn: Building a REST API with FastAPI (or Flask) over an existing service layer
Implementing simple relevance-ranked search using string matching and scoring
Using a sort with a custom key function to rank results
Writing API-level tests with a test client, separate from unit tests
steps: Install FastAPI (or Flask) and build endpoints: `POST /checkout`, `POST /return/{loan_id}`, `GET /books`, `GET /loans/{loan_id}` that call your Week 1 `LibraryService`.
Map your service's custom exceptions (`NoCopyAvailableError`, `LoanNotFoundError`) to proper HTTP status codes (409, 404) in the API layer, not inside the service.

Add a `search_books(query)` method to `LibraryService` that scores each book by: +10 for exact title match, +5 for title contains query, +3 for author contains query, using case-insensitive substring checks.
Sort search results by score descending using `sorted(..., key=..., reverse=True)`, and return the top 10 as a `GET /books/search?q=...` endpoint.
Seed the in-memory store with at least 20 varied books (overlapping words in titles/authors) so ranking behaviour is actually visible and testable.

Write API tests using FastAPI's `TestClient` (or Flask's test client) covering: checkout success, checkout with no copies (expect 409), get on unknown loan (expect 404), and a search query producing correctly ordered results.
Test that a search for a common word returns multiple books in a sensible order (exact matches before partial matches).
Commit your code with an updated README documenting the API endpoints and example requests.
deliverables: A REST API exposing checkout, return, book listing and loan lookup
Proper HTTP status code mapping from service exceptions
A scored, ranked `search_books` feature with a search endpoint
API-level tests using a test client, separate from Week 1's unit tests
done_when: `GET /books/search?q=<word>` returns results ordered with exact title matches before partial matches
Attempting to check out a book with zero available copies returns HTTP 409, not a 500 error
Looking up a nonexistent loan ID returns HTTP 404 with a clear error body
All API tests pass and are clearly separate (by file or folder) from Week 1's unit tests
hints: Keep the scoring rule simple and explicit (a small dict or if/elif chain) — the goal is applying a sort with a custom key inside a real feature, not building a search engine.
FastAPI's `TestClient` (from `fastapi.testclient`) lets you call your endpoints directly in tests without running a live server.
The [FastAPI tutorial](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/) covers path/query params and exception handlers, both directly useful this week.
2.stretch: Add pagination to `GET /books` (`?page=1&page_size=10`) and a test confirming page boundaries are correct.
post_highlights: Built a REST API over a layered service, mapping domain errors to correct HTTP status codes
Implemented ranked search with a custom scoring function and sort key
Wrote API-level tests with a test client separate from my unit test suite

3.title: Persistence, Caching and Concurrency Safety
3.goal: Swap the in-memory store for a real SQLite database, and add a small LRU-style in-memory cache for repeated lookups — applying a hash-map-backed cache data structure inside a real performance feature, plus handling concurrent checkout attempts safely.
learn: Persisting a domain model to SQLite with `sqlite3` or a lightweight ORM
Implementing a simple LRU cache using a dict plus an ordered structure
Handling a race condition: two near-simultaneous checkouts for the last copy
Writing integration tests against a real (temporary) database
steps: Design SQLite tables for `books`, `copies` and `loans` mirroring Week 1's models, and write migration/setup SQL run at startup.
Implement `SqliteBookRepository` and `SqliteLoanRepository` matching the same interface as Week 1's in-memory repositories, so `LibraryService` needs no changes to use them.
Point the API at the SQLite-backed repositories (behind a config flag or environment variable so tests can still use in-memory for speed).

Implement a small `LRUCache` class (max size, dict + doubly-linked-list or `collections.OrderedDict`) and use it to cache `search_books` results keyed by query string, invalidating the whole cache on any checkout/return.
Write a test proving the cache actually avoids re-querying the database on a repeated identical search (e.g. by counting DB calls with a mock or counter).

Simulate a race condition: write a test where two checkout calls for a book with exactly one copy left run in quick succession, and ensure only one succeeds (use a database-level constraint or a lock, not just application logic that can be beaten by timing).
Add a `sold_out` integration test hitting the real SQLite file (a temp file per test run) end to end through the service layer, not mocks.
Commit your code with an updated README describing the persistence layer, the cache, and the concurrency safeguard.
deliverables: SQLite-backed repositories implementing the same interface as the in-memory ones
A hand-implemented `LRUCache` used for search result caching with invalidation
A concurrency safeguard preventing double-checkout of the last available copy
Integration tests running against a real temporary SQLite database
done_when: Switching the config flag from in-memory to SQLite requires no changes to `LibraryService` code
A test proves the search cache is hit on a repeated identical query (fewer underlying DB calls on the second call)
A test simulating two concurrent checkouts for the last copy results in exactly one success and one clear failure, never both succeeding
Integration tests pass against a real temporary SQLite file and clean up after themselves
hints: SQLite supports `UNIQUE` constraints and transactions; a `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction around the checkout's read-then-write is a simple, real way to prevent the race condition.
`collections.OrderedDict` gives you `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)` for free, which is enough to implement LRU eviction without a custom linked list.
Use `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile` or `:memory:` SQLite carefully — file-based temp DBs are more representative of the real race-condition test.
3.stretch: Add a cache hit/miss counter exposed at `GET /stats` so you can observe cache effectiveness while using the API.
post_highlights: Swapped an in-memory repository for SQLite persistence without changing any service-layer code
Implemented a hand-written LRU cache for search results with proper invalidation
Fixed a real race condition allowing double-checkout of the last available copy

4.title: CI, Load Handling and Deployment Readiness
4.goal: Add automated CI, handle a batch-import feature efficiently using an appropriate data structure for deduplication, and get the service into a state you could actually hand off or deploy. This week is the engineering polish that makes the project real, not just working on your machine.
learn: Setting up continuous integration to run the full test suite automatically
Efficient batch processing using a set for deduplication instead of repeated linear scans
Basic structured logging and a health-check endpoint
Packaging a service for deployment (environment config, `requirements.txt`, run instructions)
steps: Set up a GitHub Actions workflow that installs dependencies and runs the full `pytest` suite (unit + API + integration) on every push.
Add a `POST /books/import` endpoint accepting a list of books (title, author, isbn) for bulk-adding, used to seed large catalogs.

Implement de-duplication in the import path using a `set` of seen ISBNs so importing a list with repeated ISBNs adds each book only once, and returns a count of skipped duplicates — avoid an O(n²) linear scan against existing books for each new one.
Write a test importing a list of 500+ books including deliberate duplicates, asserting the correct number were added versus skipped, and that it completes quickly.
Add structured logging (request method, path, status code, duration) as middleware, and a `GET /health` endpoint reporting DB connectivity and cache size.
Write a `DEPLOY.md` covering environment variables, how to run migrations, how to start the service in production mode, and how to run the test suite in CI.
Do a final review pass: remove dead code and debug prints, ensure `requirements.txt` (or `pyproject.toml`) is complete and pinned, and confirm the CI workflow passes on a fresh clone.
Record a 2-3 minute demo walking through checkout, search, the import endpoint with duplicates, and the CI run passing on GitHub.
deliverables: A working GitHub Actions CI workflow running the full test suite on push
A bulk `POST /books/import` endpoint using set-based deduplication
Structured request logging middleware and a `GET /health` endpoint
A `DEPLOY.md` and a clean, pinned dependency file
done_when: Pushing a commit triggers CI and the full test suite passes in the Actions log
Importing 500+ books with duplicate ISBNs adds each unique book exactly once and reports the correct skipped count
`GET /health` correctly reports a healthy status when the DB is reachable
A fresh clone of the repo can install dependencies and pass `pytest` using only `DEPLOY.md` and the README
hints: A `set` lookup is O(1) average case versus an O(n) scan through a list of existing ISBNs for every new book — this is the difference that matters at 500+ imported rows.
GitHub Actions' official `python-app.yml` starter workflow is a good base; you mainly need to add your dependency install and `pytest` invocation steps.
Time the import test both with and without the set-based deduplication (temporarily reverting to a linear scan) to see the real performance difference on 500+ rows.
4.stretch: Add a rate limit on `/checkout` (e.g. max 10 requests per IP per minute) using a simple in-memory token bucket, with a test confirming the 11th rapid request is rejected.
post_highlights: Set up CI so every push automatically runs the full backend test suite
Used a set for O(1) deduplication in a bulk import handling 500+ records efficiently
Got a small backend service to a real deploy-ready state with health checks and docs
